title: 2006 HMMT February Calculus Problem 3
statement: At time 0 , an ant is at \((1,0)\) and a spider is at \((-1,0)\). The ant starts walking counterclockwise along the unit circle, and the spider starts creeping to the right along the \(x\)-axis. It so happens that the ant's horizontal speed is always half the spider's. What will the shortest distance ever between the ant and the spider be?

solutions.text:
Picture an instant in time where the ant and spider have \(x\)-coordinates \(a\) and \(s\), respectively. If \(1 \leq s \leq 3\), then \(a \leq 0\), and the distance between the bugs is at least 1. If \(s>3\), then, needless to say the distance between the bugs is at least 2 . If \(-1 \leq s \leq 1\), then \(s=1-2 a\), and the distance between the bugs is

\[\sqrt{(a-(1-2 a))^{2}+\left(1-a^{2}\right)}=\sqrt{8 a^{2}-6 a+2}=\sqrt{\frac{(8 a-3)^{2}+7}{8}}\]

which attains the minimum value of \(\sqrt{7 / 8}\) when \(a=3 / 8\).
